opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting tensions in the field right now. If you look at where the progress has come from, there are roughly two camps. One is the vision-language-action line of work, where you take a big pretrained vision-language model and teach it to output actions. Those models are great at semantic generalization. You can say "pick up the extinct animal" and it'll grab the toy dinosaur, because it inherits all that internet knowledge. But the motions tend to be fairly coarse: pick and place, pushing things around, opening drawers.

Then on the other side you have the really dexterous results: diffusion policies, action chunking, high-frequency control trained on teleoperated data. You see robots folding laundry, tying shoelaces, inserting things with tight tolerances. Those are impressive, but they're often trained on a narrow task distribution, and if you change the instruction or the scene meaningfully, they don't carry over the way you'd hope.

So the room for improvement is really in bringing those together, and I think there are a few bottlenecks.

The first is data. Dexterous data is expensive. You need skilled teleoperators, good hardware, and lots of hours, and that data rarely comes paired with rich, diverse language. Most of it is labeled "fold the shirt" ten thousand times. So the model never learns how language maps onto the fine-grained variation in the motion. We need better ways to annotate data with language after the fact, using VLMs to densely caption trajectories, and to collect data that varies the instruction rather than just the scene.

The second is architecture. There's a real mismatch in time scales. Language reasoning happens slowly, maybe a few hertz, while dexterous control needs to be tens to hundreds of hertz with very precise continuous outputs. A lot of the recent progress, things like the dual-system approaches where a slower reasoning model conditions a fast action expert, points in the right direction. But I think we're still early in figuring out the right interface between the two: what representation passes from the "thinking" part to the "doing" part so that the low-level controller actually respects the nuance in the instruction.

The third is that we under-use cross-embodiment and human data. Humans do dexterous things with language attached all the time, on video. If we can learn better from egocentric human video and transfer that to robot hands, that could unlock a lot of the generalization without needing a teleoperator for every skill.

And finally, evaluation. It's honestly hard to measure this well. Most benchmarks test either generalization or dexterity, rarely both at once. Until we have evaluations that ask "can you do this precise thing, in a new setting, from a novel instruction," it's hard to know whether we're actually closing the gap or just moving along one axis.

So I'm optimistic, but I think the next real leap comes from treating dexterity and instruction following as one problem rather than bolting a language model onto a motor policy.

r001.rationale: The response calls combining dexterity and instruction following/generalization a key unresolved challenge, contrasting broad semantic generalization with dexterous skills that transfer poorly.

r002.rationale: It says current benchmarks rarely test dexterity and generalization together and calls for evaluations of precise actions in new settings from novel instructions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we've gotten pretty good at two of those three things at a time, and the hard part is getting all three to show up in the same policy at once.

If you look at the field right now, you can find systems that are remarkably dexterous. They can do really fine-grained manipulation, things like folding, tying, inserting, handling deformables. But those systems tend to be trained on a narrow distribution, often a single scene, a single embodiment, a fixed set of objects. Then on the other side you have these large vision-language-action models that generalize beautifully. You can walk them into a new kitchen, point at an object they've never seen, give them a natural language instruction, and they'll do something sensible. But the actual motor behavior is often coarse. They'll pick and place, they'll open a drawer, but they won't do the delicate, contact-rich stuff reliably.

So the first place I see room for improvement is just closing that gap. A lot of it comes down to data. Dexterity requires high-frequency, high-quality demonstrations with real contact information, and generalization requires breadth across scenes and objects and tasks. Those two kinds of data are expensive in different ways, and historically the datasets have been collected by different communities with different priorities. I think the most promising direction is figuring out how to let the broad, internet-scale knowledge from vision and language actually transfer into the low-level motor controller rather than just sitting on top of it as a planner.

The second thing is instruction following, and I'd argue it's still kind of shallow in most systems. The model can map "pick up the red cup" to the right object, which is great, but the instruction doesn't really modulate how the task is done. If I say "gently" or "quickly" or "without spilling," a human immediately changes their motor behavior. Most robot policies either ignore that or treat it as a lookup into a few discrete modes. Getting language to actually condition the fine-grained dynamics of the motion, not just the goal, is a big open problem and I think it's where a lot of the real value is going to come from.

And then there's the architectural question underneath all of this. There's been a lot of debate about whether you want one monolithic model that does everything end to end, or a hierarchy where a big semantic model does the reasoning and hands off to a smaller, fast, dexterous controller. I actually think the hierarchical approach is a pragmatic bridge, and it's where a lot of the strong results are coming from today. But the interface between the two levels is a bit of a lossy bottleneck. You lose information when you compress down to a subgoal or a language string. So the long-term thing I'd want to see is architectures where the high-level reasoning and the low-level control share representations more directly, so that generalization in one actually improves the other instead of them being bolted together.

The last piece I'd flag is evaluation. We don't really have good benchmarks that stress all three capabilities simultaneously. Most evals are either dexterity benchmarks on a fixed setup or generalization benchmarks with easy motor skills. Until we're measuring the combination, it's hard to know if we're actually making progress on the combination, versus just getting better at each axis independently and hoping they compose.

r001.rationale: The response describes closing the gap between highly dexterous systems and broadly generalizing systems as a key open problem.

r002.rationale: It says current evaluations tend to test dexterity or generalization separately and calls for benchmarks that stress all three capabilities together.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of room for improvement at the intersection of those capabilities. You can have a robot that’s very dexterous on a particular task, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can handle a different object or understand a new instruction. And you can have a model that understands what you’re asking for, but doesn’t have the fine-grained control to execute it reliably.

So the challenge is connecting that high-level understanding to the physical interaction. If I say, “Pick this up gently,” gently has to mean something in terms of how the robot approaches the object, how much force it applies, and how it responds when the object starts slipping. It can’t just be a language-level concept.

I think a big opportunity is to train and evaluate those capabilities together. Can the robot perform a precise manipulation with an unfamiliar object? Can it adapt when you change the instruction? And when something goes wrong, can it use feedback to recover? That’s the kind of generalization we want: understanding the goal and continually adjusting its actions to achieve it.

r001.rationale: It describes a gap at the intersection of dexterity and generalization, noting that skill on one task does not ensure performance with new objects or instructions.

r002.rationale: It calls for training and evaluating these capabilities together and gives evaluation questions about precise manipulation with unfamiliar objects and adapting to changed instructions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a pretty big gap between being able to understand an instruction and having the physical skills to execute it. A model might understand what you mean by “clean up the kitchen,” but that doesn’t mean it can reliably pick up a slippery plate, manipulate something fragile, or recover when an object moves unexpectedly.

One opportunity is to connect the broad understanding you get from vision-language models with policies that have learned rich, precise motor behavior. You want the robot to generalize to a new object or a new instruction without losing the dexterity that makes the behavior work in the real world.

And I think we need to evaluate those capabilities together. Can the robot follow an unfamiliar instruction, manipulate unfamiliar objects, and recover from mistakes over a longer task? That combination is much closer to what we actually want from a useful robot.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between broad instruction understanding and physical execution, and calls for combining generalizing vision-language understanding with precise motor skills.

r002.rationale: It says to evaluate these capabilities together, including following unfamiliar instructions and manipulating unfamiliar objects, which tests whether dexterous behavior generalizes.
